vt_pisgah_crag.blurb: Pisgah Crag is the ice and mixed face on the east side of Lake Willoughby in Westmore, Vermont. It is a winter objective first: the large majority of the climbs here are water ice, most of them around WI5, with a smaller group at WI4 and a single WI6. A few rock and mixed lines round it out. Expect long, committing lines, often several pitches, above a quiet and remote-feeling lake. The rock is often buried under ice in season, and the way in is a hike up talus from the road, which is awkward without boots that grip well. Short winter days reward an early start.

va_tunnel_turret_wall.blurb: Tunnel Turret Wall is the first big cluster of climbing on the Guest River Gorge rail trail near Coeburn in southwest Virginia, reached by walking the flat old railbed through a former coal train tunnel. The wall is mostly bolted, with a smaller set of trad lines, and the grades spread widely: a few easy 5.6 to 5.8 climbs, a deep middle of 5.9 and 5.10, and a handful reaching into 5.12 and 5.13. Because the trail is flat and gravel, the walk-in is easy for a mixed group, and a bike speeds up the trip to farther sectors of the gorge.
va_tunnel_turret_wall.parking_note: Leave the car in the gorge trailhead lot, the one approved spot for the climbing. From Coeburn, take Route 72 south to the Forest Service turn; the lot lies at the end of the access road, a bit beyond the Flatwoods picnic area.
va_tunnel_turret_wall.approach: Follow the flat gravel railbed from the lot and pass through the old coal train tunnel. The wall is at the first mile marker along the trail.

va_big_shot.blurb: Big Shot is a bolted wall at the third mile marker of the Guest River Gorge trail near Coeburn, Virginia, among the harder walls in the gorge. Every climb here is a sport route, and the grades skew difficult: the bulk are 5.12 and 5.13, with a smaller group of 5.10s and 5.11s as a way in. Expect a longer walk than at the first-mile walls, along the flat gravel railbed, which is easy to bike. It sits near other Mile Three walls, so a day can link several of them. Come ready for sustained climbing, as there is little here for beginners.
va_big_shot.parking_note: Park in the gorge trailhead lot, the one approved spot for the climbing. From Coeburn, take Route 72 south to the Forest Service turn; the lot is at the end of the access road past the Flatwoods picnic area.
va_big_shot.approach: Walk or bike the flat gravel railbed from the lot, through the old coal train tunnel, to the third mile marker, a few miles in.

va_main_crag.blurb: Main Crag is the principal cliff at Love Gap, off the Blue Ridge Parkway near Charlottesville. It is a modest, mostly trad crag of granite that is often decomposed, so expect some loose rock and wear a helmet. Climbs are friction, slab and crack lines, mainly between 5.6 and 5.10, with a good number of boulder problems at the base as well. Routes tend to wander, and protection can be thin on the easier ground. The face looks southwest and catches plenty of sun, which suits the cooler seasons; summer runs hot and humid.
va_main_crag.parking_note: Take the Parkway to milepost 16 and turn onto gravel Campbell's Mountain Road (Route 814). A little under half a mile along is a small, often muddy pullout beside a driveway, easy to drive past.
va_main_crag.approach: Cross the road and take the rough path that leaves the old logging track to the left. It reaches the base in about five minutes, though the rock is hard to spot once trees leaf out.

va_buzzard_rocks.blurb: Buzzard Rocks is a west-facing slab crag on a ridge above the Fort Valley at Elizabeth Furnace, in George Washington National Forest. Climbs are mostly trad with a number of bolted routes, a few top-ropes and some boulder problems, on slabby faces with big views down into the valley. Grades cluster at 5.7 and 5.8, with a smaller group at 5.10. Expect a real walk-in, a long climb up the ridge of around 45 minutes, and carry water, since there is none at the cliff. The face stays shaded into the afternoon, so summer mornings and winter afternoons are comfortable.
va_buzzard_rocks.parking_note: A small dirt lot at the trailhead fills early on busy days, with a little overflow room just beyond it.
va_buzzard_rocks.approach: A steady trail of about two miles climbs to the ridge. The last stretch is steep and ends in switchbacks, then a short walk along the ridgeline leads to side paths dropping to each group of routes.

va_lower_lodges.blurb: Lower Lodges is a sunny sport-climbing wall below the Lodges cliff at Breaks Interstate Park, on the Virginia and Kentucky line. The routes are overwhelmingly bolted, with just a few trad lines, and the grades sit in the middle to hard range: most are 5.10 and 5.11, with a good number of 5.12s and only a handful of easier climbs. The wall catches the sun, so it is a good choice for cooler days. The hike in is short, roughly ten minutes through the woods from the Lodges lot along a climber trail, with flagging marking some turns.
va_lower_lodges.parking_note: Use the Lodges parking lot at Breaks Interstate Park; the trail heads into the woods from the lot.

va_talking_headwall.blurb: Talking Headwall is a small roadside crag at Elizabeth Furnace in George Washington National Forest, in the Fort Valley near Waterlick, Virginia. Most routes are bolted on a steep, overhanging wall with generous holds, alongside some trad lines and a few boulder problems. Grades run from easy to 5.12, with the largest group at 5.10. The wall is shaded in the morning and warms quickly later, and a swimming hole at the base is welcome in summer. It is popular with groups, so arriving early helps, and a stick clip is handy for the first bolts.
va_talking_headwall.parking_note: Roadside paved pullout on Fort Valley Road (VA-678), 1.8 miles from the Route 55 junction, with space for about eight vehicles. The cliff slips past quickly when driving, so watch for it.
va_talking_headwall.approach: A short stroll back along the pavement, about 200 yards, leads to a well-worn path up to the base.

va_olympus_boulder.blurb: Olympus is the signature boulder of the Picnic Area at Grayson Highlands State Park in southwest Virginia, set among old rhododendron just steps from the parking lot. It is a huge overhanging block, roughly eighteen feet tall and seventy-plus feet long, with steep main lines through the middle and shorter, more moderate problems along its sides. Problems range from V2 into the V13 range, spread fairly evenly across the middle grades. The overhang keeps it shaded through the day and the park sits high, around 5,000 feet, so it is a summer destination. A restroom and playground nearby suit mixed groups.
va_olympus_boulder.parking_note: Turn right at the Picnic Area sign just past the park entrance station; the boulder is a short stroll from the lot.
va_olympus_boulder.approach: Under a minute on foot from the lot.
